entries.meaning: Bhushundi tells Garuda that he has sung the Lord's glory according to his own understanding, not through special ingenuity: he has seen it with his own eyes. Raghunatha's name, form, virtues and story are immeasurable and endless; sages praise them according to their insight, while the Vedas, Shesha and Shiva cannot reach their limit. As birds from Garuda down to a gnat fly in the sky without finding its end, no one can sound the depths of Raghupati's glory. Rama's body possesses the beauty of hundreds of millions of Kamadevas, the power to crush foes of countless Durgas, the splendour of hundreds of millions of Indras and the vastness of countless skies.

The Lord has the depth of countless netherworlds and the dread power of hundreds of millions of Yamas. He is as purifying as innumerable pilgrimage places, while his name destroys every mass of sin. Raghubira is as immovable as countless Himalayas, as profound as hundreds of millions of oceans and, like countless wish-fulfilling cows, grants every desire. His intelligence equals countless Sarasvatis; his creative skill, hundreds of millions of Brahmas; his sustaining power, countless Vishnus; and his power of dissolution, hundreds of millions of Rudras. He possesses the wealth of countless Kuberas, is the source of countless manifestations of Maya and bears the earth with the power of hundreds of millions of Sheshas. The Lord of the world is limitless and beyond comparison.

Hearing Bhushundi's beautiful words, Garuda rejoices and his feathers stand on end. Tears fill his eyes as Raghupati's glory enters his heart. Remembering his former delusion, he regrets having taken the beginningless Brahman to be merely human; again and again he bows at the crow-sage's feet and, recognizing his Rama-like love, grows more devoted. No one crosses the ocean of becoming without a guru, even one equal to Brahma or Shiva. Garuda says that the serpent of doubt had swallowed him and waves of painful false reasoning had overwhelmed him; Bhushundi's very form became the antidote and Raghunayaka, giver of joy to servants, restored him to life. By Bhushundi's grace his delusion has vanished and he has understood Rama's incomparable mystery.

Garuda praises Bhushundi as all-knowing, beyond darkness, wise, gentle and straightforward—the dwelling of knowledge, detachment and realization and a beloved servant of Raghunayaka. He asks why Bhushundi received a crow's body and where he found the beautiful lake of Rama's story. Shiva, Garuda says, has declared that even the great dissolution does not destroy Bhushundi; since Ishvara does not speak in vain, this remains a wonder in Garuda's mind. All moving and unmoving beings—serpents, humans and gods—are food for Time, while mighty Time dissolves innumerable cosmic shells and is always impossible to overcome; Garuda asks for the whole explanation.

Hearing Garuda, the crow-sage rejoices and speaks with profound love. He calls Garuda's question blessed and dear, for it recalls the memory of his many births, and asks him to listen attentively while he tells his own story. Repetition, austerity, sacrifice, restraint, vows, charity, detachment, discernment, yoga and realization all culminate in love for Raghupati's feet; without that love no one finds lasting well-being. Bhushundi obtained devotion to Rama in his present body and therefore cherishes it deeply, because everyone naturally loves that through which one's true good is gained.

A being's true self-interest is love for Rama's feet in thought, word and deed. Only a body used to worship Raghubira is pure and fortunate; poets and the learned do not praise even a Brahma-like body turned away from Rama. Devotion arose in Bhushundi's heart in this crow-body, so it is supremely dear to him and, because he can die at will, he does not abandon it; scripture does not prescribe embodied worship without a body. Delusion once ruined him, and one turned from Rama never sleeps in happiness. Through many births he performed many acts—yoga, repetition, austerity, sacrifice and charity—and wandered through every kind of womb, but no deed made him as happy as he is now. By Shiva's grace he remembers those many births and delusion no longer encloses his understanding.

In one Kali age Bhushundi went to Ayodhya and was born in a Shudra body. He served Shiva in thought, word and deed, but proudly reviled other deities; intoxicated by wealth, talkative, harsh-minded and deeply hypocritical, he did not understand the glory of Raghupati's capital. He now knows Ayodhya's power as sung by Veda, Agama and Purana: whoever dwells there in any birth ultimately becomes devoted to Rama. A person understands Ayodhya's power when bow-bearing Rama dwells in the heart. That Kali age was severe, and men and women were bent on sin.

Bhushundi describes Kali-age disorder: the duties of social orders and the four stages of life disappear, and people delight in opposing revelation. Brahmins sell scripture, rulers prey upon their subjects and no one respects Vedic discipline. Whatever path pleases someone is called right; whoever talks loudly is called learned; ostentatious hypocrites are called saints. A thief of another's wealth is called clever, a pretender a great exemplar and a practised liar and jester virtuous. One who abandons scriptural conduct is acclaimed as a knower and renunciant, while long nails and matted hair alone make a celebrated ascetic.

He continues the Kali-age portrait: men become subservient to women and dance like an actor's monkey. Shudras instruct Brahmins, don sacred threads and accept improper gifts. People are absorbed in desire, greed and anger and oppose gods, Brahmins, scripture and saints. Unfortunate women abandon virtuous and handsome husbands for other men; married women lack ornaments while widows adopt novel adornment. Guru and disciple resemble the deaf and blind—one does not listen and the other does not see. A guru who takes a disciple's wealth but does not remove sorrow falls into terrible hell. Parents call children only to teach that filling the belly is the whole of dharma.

Libertines, deceivers, the deluded, hostile and possessive pose as nondual sages; Bhushundi says he saw such Kali-age conduct himself. Having fallen, they also ruin any who follow the true path. Those who attack scripture with sophistry fall into a separate hell for an age. People from occupations then ranked low—oil pressers, potters, hunters, forest communities, distillers and others—lose wife or property, shave their heads, become renunciants and demand worship from Brahmins, destroying both worlds for themselves. Unlettered, greedy and lustful Brahmins abandon conduct, while Shudras perform recitations, austerities and vows and expound Puranas from elevated seats. Everyone invents practices; the boundless disorder cannot be described.
